standard.title: Changing Perspectives on Migration
standard.description: the causes of changes in perspectives, responses, beliefs and values on migration that have influenced Australian society since 1945
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined successive migration waves and their effects on Australian society in K07. They understand the 'White Australia' policy as a boundary condition and know that it was dismantled between the late 1960s and 1973. They have not yet examined the specific causes of attitudinal change toward migration, the arguments over multiculturalism, or how contemporary immigration policy debates evolved.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse the causes of changes in perspectives on migration since 1945, including the dismantling of the White Australia policy, the contribution of migration to Australia's changing identity, and the evolution of contemporary immigration debates.

nodes.label: The White Australia policy — logic, operation, and dismantling
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the ideological basis and operation of the White Australia policy and analyse the causes of its gradual dismantling between the late 1960s and 1973.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain the logic of the White Australia policy; identify at least two causes of its dismantling.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine the White Australia policy's ideological foundations (racial hierarchy, fear of Asian labour competition, British identity); its operation through the Immigration Restriction Act 1901 and the dictation test; the arguments for and against the policy as it came under pressure (economic development needs, Cold War alliance politics, Asian diplomatic relationships, changing global norms post-Holocaust and UDHR); trace its gradual dismantling — Holt's 1966 changes, Whitlam's final abolition in 1973.
wider: Examine the role of Cold War diplomacy in eroding the White Australia policy — analysing how Australia's relationships with non-white Asian allies (South Korea, South Vietnam, Malaysia) made overt racial exclusion increasingly untenable

Investigate the arguments of those who defended the policy to the end — analysing what values and fears they expressed, and what this reveals about the gap between official ideology and social attitudes
nodes.hinge_reason: The White Australia policy's logic and dismantling is the structural context for understanding all subsequent attitudinal change toward migration. Students who do not understand why the policy existed and how it was argued away cannot analyse the causes of changing perspectives — they can only describe that attitudes changed.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat the White Australia policy as obviously wrong and its dismantling as obviously inevitable. The scaffold is: what was the internal logic of the policy for those who supported it? what specific forces eroded that logic? This makes the change analytically explicable rather than morally self-evident.

success_criteria: Explains the ideological basis of the White Australia policy — not merely that it was discriminatory
Identifies at least two distinct causes of its dismantling and explains the mechanism of each
Traces the key steps in dismantling from Holt (1966) to Whitlam (1973)

nodes.label: Changing attitudes to migrants — decade by decade
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how Australian public attitudes to migration changed across the 1950s–1980s, using sources to identify shifts in perspective and explain their causes.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two shifts in public attitudes to migration across the post-war period and explain the cause of each shift.
nodes.typical_width: Students use primary and secondary sources to trace changing attitudes — initial ambivalence toward European 'New Australians' in the 1950s; growing acceptance as assimilation proceeded; rising concern as Asian migration increased in the 1970s; the multiculturalism debate of the 1980s (Galbally Report, Fraser government policy); examine how media representation, political rhetoric, and social contact shaped attitudes at each stage; explain the causes of attitudinal shifts in terms of changing migrant sources, policy changes, and international context.
wider: Examine the 1988 Fitzgerald Report on immigration as a moment of policy contestation — analysing how it both responded to and shaped public attitudes
Investigate the sources used to trace attitudes — newspaper editorials, survey data, political speeches — and evaluate each source type's strengths and limitations for analysing public opinion
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The source analysis task — using multiple source types to trace attitudinal change — is a rich application of AC9HH10S03 and S04 skills. Examining how different source types capture different dimensions of public opinion builds genuine historical methodology skills.

response_modes.reason: Tracking attitudes decade by decade prevents overgeneralisation — 'Australians were racist' or 'Australians gradually became tolerant' — and builds the evidential basis for explaining causes rather than outcomes.

success_criteria: Describes at least two shifts in public attitudes to migration across the post-war period
Explains the cause of each identified shift — not merely notes that it occurred
Uses at least two different source types to support the analysis

nodes.label: Migration and Australian identity — the multiculturalism debate
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the contribution of migration to Australia's changing national identity and analyse the debate over multiculturalism that emerged in the 1980s.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain how migration contributed to Australia's changing identity; identify at least one argument for and one against multiculturalism as a policy and social framework.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine how successive waves of migration transformed Australia's cultural, religious, and demographic composition; explain the emergence of multiculturalism as both a social reality and a government policy (Fraser government, Galbally Report 1978); analyse the debate over multiculturalism — arguments that it enriched Australian society and strengthened its international relationships versus arguments that it fragmented national cohesion and failed to integrate migrants adequately; connect to the ongoing debate over Australian identity.
wider: Compare Australia's multiculturalism model with Canada's — examining whether the two countries took different approaches to managing diversity and what produced different outcomes

Examine First Nations Australians' relationship to multiculturalism — analysing whether a framework designed for migrant diversity adequately recognises the distinct status of First Nations peoples as the original inhabitants
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The comparison with Canada and the First Nations–multiculturalism relationship are analytically rich directions that extend the identity question beyond a simple celebration-versus-critique binary.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat multiculturalism as either obviously good or obviously contested without examining the specific arguments on each side. Scaffolding both the case for and the case against — using evidence — builds genuine analytical engagement rather than position-stating.

success_criteria: Explains how migration contributed to Australia's changing national identity with specific examples
Identifies at least one argument for and one against multiculturalism as a framework — with evidence
Explains multiculturalism as both a social reality and a government policy — distinguishing the two

nodes.label: Contemporary immigration debates — continuity and change in attitudes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how immigration and border protection debates have evolved from the 1990s to the present, connecting contemporary debates to the longer history of Australian attitudes to migration.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two contemporary immigration policy debates and explain how each connects to earlier patterns in Australian attitudes to migration.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine the evolution of debates from the 1990s — mandatory detention of asylum seekers, the Tampa affair, the Pacific Solution, temporary protection visas, humanitarian migration, business and skilled migration; explain how each debate reflects a continuity or change in the attitudes traced in N1–N3; evaluate whether contemporary debates represent a new phase in Australian immigration attitudes or a recurrence of earlier patterns.
wider: Examine the One Nation movement (from 1996) as a case study in the political mobilisation of anti-immigration sentiment — analysing how it drew on longstanding anxieties and how mainstream parties responded

Evaluate the contemporary debate over asylum seekers using the push-pull framework from K07 — analysing whether 'boat people' are best understood as economic migrants or refugees, and what the distinction reveals about how Australia's obligations are framed

response_modes.reason: This node draws together the policy history (N1), attitudinal shifts (N2), and identity debate (N3) into an account of how contemporary immigration debates are shaped by the longer history. Tasks requiring students to connect a contemporary debate to an earlier historical pattern work well here.

success_criteria: Describes at least two contemporary immigration policy debates with specific evidence
Connects each debate to an earlier pattern in Australian attitudes to migration
Evaluates whether contemporary debates represent continuity or change — with a supported argument
